strengths: The paper identifies an important and under-discussed issue in class-incremental learning evaluation: performance can vary substantially with class/task order, and reporting only a few random seeds can hide poor worst-case behavior.

The proposed EDGE protocol is simple, computationally cheap, and practically motivated: using semantic inter-task similarity to construct easy and hard sequences is an intuitive way to stress-test CIL methods.

The empirical study covers a fairly broad set of CIL methods, including both pretrained and non-pretrained approaches, and reports distributional metrics such as Jensen-Shannon divergence and Wasserstein distance rather than only average accuracy.
The enumerable experiments provide useful evidence that random-seed evaluation can misestimate lower and upper performance bounds, sometimes changing conclusions about model robustness.
weaknesses: The central theoretical analysis appears unsound in places. In particular, Theorem 2 assumes that adding two extreme sequences yields an unbiased estimator of the true mean, but the estimator weights the selected extremes differently from their population mass and need not have expectation equal to the population mean. This undermines the claimed sample-complexity improvement.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The paper repeatedly claims approximation of the full performance distribution, but EDGE uses only three sequences and mainly targets extremes; fitting a Gaussian from such samples is fragile, especially when normality is only argued after Box-Cox transformation on tiny enumerable settings.

The main quantitative validation of distributional accuracy is limited to 6 classes and 3 tasks, yielding only 90 sequences. This is far from standard CIL settings, and it is unclear whether conclusions scale to 100 or 200 classes where the true distribution cannot be checked.

The standard CIL experiments do not have ground-truth bounds, so showing that EDGE finds lower minima and higher maxima than RS does not by itself prove that these are accurate or representative distributional estimates.

The reliance on CLIP text-label similarity may fail for datasets where class names are ambiguous, visually misleading, fine-grained, or not semantically aligned with transfer/forgetting dynamics. The paper gives limited ablation of alternative similarity measures or failure cases.

The comparison baseline is weak: RS with three fixed seeds is common but not the only reasonable protocol. The paper should compare against larger random budgets, stratified sampling, adversarial/curriculum orderings, image-feature similarity, and recent order-robust/dynamic benchmarking methods more directly.

Some mathematical and algorithmic statements are questionable or imprecise, such as the claim that a randomly selected median sequence is theoretically guaranteed to lie near the center, and the proof steps connecting semantic similarity to generalization error rely on strong proportionality assumptions that are not justified.

Presentation and reproducibility have notable issues: several figures/tables are difficult to read in the extracted manuscript, the abstract has an incomplete code URL, and some references/citations appear incorrect or duplicated.

strengths: The paper raises a relevant and under-discussed issue: class-incremental learning results can depend strongly on class/task order, and reporting only a few random seeds can hide worst-case behavior.
The proposed use of semantically informed easy/hard task orders is intuitive and could be useful as a robustness diagnostic alongside conventional random-order evaluation.

The empirical section covers several CIL methods across pretrained and non-pretrained families, and the small enumerable setting provides some evidence that random sampling can miss performance extremes.
weaknesses: The central theoretical support appears unsound. In Theorem 2, the estimator that forcibly includes two extreme sequences is not generally centered at the true population mean, yet the proof states its martingale expectation equals the true mean. This undermines the claimed guarantee that extreme sampling improves distribution estimation.

The method conflates robustness stress testing with estimating the true random-order performance distribution. Deliberately selecting easy and hard sequences can reveal bounds, but using only hard/easy/random samples to estimate a Gaussian mean and variance is statistically unjustified and can be biased by construction.

The empirical validation of distribution estimation is very limited: the only exhaustive ground truth uses 6 classes and 3 tasks, while the standard CIL experiments have no ground-truth distribution and therefore cannot verify that EDGE estimates the real distribution better.

The assumption that CIL performance is Gaussian is weakly supported. The paper applies Box-Cox transformations and normality tests on tiny enumerable settings, which does not establish that the original performance distribution in realistic settings is Gaussian or that three samples are sufficient to fit it.

Several theoretical arguments rely on unsupported links between CLIP text-label similarity, task parameter distances, and CIL generalization error. The proof of the similarity-performance relationship contains strong proportionality/conservation assumptions that are not justified for real CIL models.

The comparison to random sampling is not sufficiently rigorous. EDGE is compared mainly against one fixed three-seed RS protocol; stronger baselines such as many random draws, stratified sampling, search over random candidates, uncertainty estimates, or adversarial/curriculum order construction are missing.

Some results are mixed or overstated. Tables show cases where EDGE is worse than RS on some metrics, yet the paper frames the outcome as broadly consistent. The standard-setting experiments mostly demonstrate that EDGE selects more extreme sequences, which is expected by design, not that it provides a calibrated evaluation protocol.

Reproducibility and presentation have issues: the abstract says code is available but the link appears missing, important algorithmic details are deferred or ambiguous, figures/tables are hard to read in places, and there is little discussion of limitations or failure modes.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-discussed problem in class-incremental learning: evaluation can be highly sensitive to class order, and reporting averages over only a few random sequences can hide poor worst-case behavior.
The core idea of explicitly evaluating easy and hard class sequences is practically useful, especially for robustness-oriented model selection.
The manuscript includes a broad empirical comparison across many CIL methods, covering both pre-trained and non-pre-trained settings, and reports distributional metrics beyond mean accuracy.
The enumerable 6-class/3-task experiments are a valuable diagnostic setting because they allow comparison against a true sequence-performance distribution.
The presentation is generally clear, with intuitive figures and tables that make the evaluation-protocol issue easy to understand.
weaknesses: Several theoretical claims appear unsound or overstated. In particular, Theorem 1 introduces a log |Omega| factor through an unjustified union bound even though estimating a bounded population mean by random sampling should not require dependence on the size of the sequence space in this way.

Theorem 2 is problematic: the proposed estimator that includes two extreme sequences is generally biased for the population mean, yet the proof sets its expectation equal to the true mean. This undermines the claimed sample-complexity advantage of extreme-sequence-assisted estimation.

The link between CLIP text similarity and CIL performance extremes is only weakly supported. The reported Pearson correlations in Figure 2c appear small for several methods, yet the paper describes the relationship as strong and consistent.

EDGE uses deliberately selected hard/easy sequences plus one random sequence, but it is unclear why fitting or summarizing a full performance distribution from these three biased samples should yield an accurate estimate of mean and variance. The method is more convincing as a boundary-probing protocol than as a distribution-estimation protocol.

The strongest quantitative validation relies on very small enumerable settings with only six selected classes and 90 sequences. It is not clear that conclusions transfer to full CIFAR-100, CUB-200, or ImageNet-R settings where true distributional boundaries are unknown.

The classic CIL experiments mainly show that EDGE finds wider lower/upper ranges than random sampling, but without exhaustive or stronger approximate ground truth this does not prove that those are true extremes or that the estimated distribution is better.

Important ablations are missing or underdeveloped, such as comparisons to larger random-sampling budgets, multiple random seeds beyond the conventional three, image-feature similarity, WordNet/label hierarchy similarity, exhaustive search in the enumerable setting, or simple adversarial/random-hard baselines.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, especially around Gaussianity of the true distribution, theoretical guarantees for the median/random sequence, and the reliability of EDGE for estimating full performance distributions.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-examined issue in class-incremental learning: performance can vary substantially with class order, and reporting only a few random orders can hide worst-case behavior.
EDGE is simple, computationally cheap, and easy to integrate: constructing hard/easy orders from CLIP text similarities is a practical idea that could be useful as an additional stress-test protocol.

The empirical section covers many CIL methods across pretrained and non-pretrained settings, and the small enumerable experiments provide a useful attempt to compare against a ground-truth sequence distribution.
The paper is generally readable and includes appendices with pseudo-code, additional baselines, robustness checks over CLIP backbones, and repository usage details.
weaknesses: Several theoretical claims appear overstated or technically questionable. For example, estimating a bounded mean by random sampling does not generally require sample complexity scaling with log |Omega| in the way argued, and the union-bound motivation is unclear for a scalar mean estimate.

Theorem 2 appears problematic: adding known extreme sequences to an estimator generally biases the mean unless special conditions hold, yet the proof effectively treats the estimator expectation as the true mean. This weakens the claimed theoretical basis for extreme-assisted distribution estimation.

Theorem 3 relies on strong and insufficiently justified assumptions linking CLIP/text semantic similarity, parameter distances, and generalization error. The empirical correlations shown are often weak, so the claim that similarity reliably orders hard/random/easy sequences is stronger than the evidence supports.

The strongest ground-truth evaluation is very small: only six classes split into three tasks, yielding 90 sequences. This is useful diagnostically but may not reflect standard CIL regimes with many classes/tasks, different class taxonomies, or more complex order effects.

In standard large-scale settings, the paper mostly shows that EDGE finds more extreme values than three random seeds, but without ground truth it is hard to know whether EDGE better estimates the true distribution or simply produces a deliberately wider, potentially biased distribution.

The protocol fits a Gaussian from three non-i.i.d. samples consisting of hard, random, and easy sequences. This is not a statistically well-justified estimator of the true performance distribution, especially when the sampling scheme is intentionally biased toward extremes.

The method depends heavily on semantic similarity from class names or generated captions. The paper acknowledges domain issues, but the solution using LLM-generated captions introduces additional dependencies and potential instability, and the evidence is limited.

Positioning could be sharper relative to robust/adversarial/order-aware evaluation methods. Some additional baselines are included in the appendix, but the main paper still centers mostly on comparison to the weak three-seed RS protocol.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-discussed issue: CIL results can be highly sensitive to class order, and reporting only a few random seeds can be misleading.
The high-level idea of explicitly evaluating easy and hard class sequences is intuitive and potentially useful for robustness-oriented model assessment.
The authors evaluate a reasonably broad set of CIL methods across pretrained and non-pretrained regimes, and include both enumerable toy settings and larger standard settings.
weaknesses: The main theoretical claims appear technically unsound. In particular, Theorem 2 treats the estimator including two extreme samples as if its expectation were the full-population mean, but sampling from the remaining space with fixed extremes generally gives a biased estimator unless special conditions hold. This undermines the claimed sample-efficiency argument.

Theorem 1 is not a convincing critique of estimating a mean: the proof introduces an unnecessary union bound over the sequence space, inflating the sample complexity. The result does not establish that random sampling is fundamentally inadequate for all relevant estimands.

Theorem 3 is weakly justified and relies on strong, informal assumptions connecting CLIP label similarity, task similarity, parameter distances, generalization error, and CIL accuracy. The proof does not convincingly establish the claimed monotonic ordering of hard, random, and easy sequences.

The empirical support for the core method is narrow. The only setting with ground-truth distributions uses the first six classes split into three tasks, yielding only 90 sequences; this is too small and arbitrary to validate claims about realistic CIL evaluation.

The larger benchmark experiments lack ground truth distributions, so showing that EDGE finds lower minima and higher maxima than random sampling mostly confirms the method is designed to search for extremes, not that it estimates the true distribution more accurately.

The paper overstates the Gaussian/distribution-estimation framing. Normality is assumed in the main text, later supported only partially and sometimes after transformations; three samples cannot meaningfully estimate a full distribution.

Baselines are insufficient. The paper mainly compares against three-seed random sampling, but should include stronger alternatives such as more random samples under equal/varied budgets, stratified sampling, diversity-based sequence selection, CLIP-similarity randomization, image-feature similarity, and oracle/near-oracle search in enumerable settings.
Several reported interpretations are overstated. For example, the similarity-performance correlations shown are quite small for many methods, yet are used to motivate a broad causal/evaluative claim.

The proposed protocol may conflate evaluation with a CLIP/text-label prior. It is unclear whether label-name similarity is reliable for fine-grained, ambiguous, non-English, domain-specific, or visually dissimilar classes, and the paper does not sufficiently analyze such failure modes.

Reproducibility and presentation have issues: the abstract says code is available but appears to omit the link, and there are multiple notation, formatting, and clarity problems that make the method and claims harder to verify.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and under-discussed weakness in class-incremental learning evaluation: reporting averages over only a few random class orders can hide substantial order-dependent variance and worst-case failures.

The proposed EDGE protocol is simple, practical, and well motivated: using inter-task similarity to construct hard/easy sequences is an appealing way to obtain more informative evaluations without exhaustive enumeration.

Empirical coverage is fairly broad, including pretrained and non-pretrained CIL methods, CIFAR-100, CUB, and ImageNet-R, with additional appendices on CLIP encoders, alternative baselines, random-sampling budgets, and repository usage.
The enumerable experiments clearly show that random sampling can misestimate lower/upper bounds and model rankings, while EDGE often better captures extremes and distributional spread.

The paper is relevant and potentially useful to the continual learning community because it proposes an evaluation protocol rather than another model, and it could improve robustness reporting in future CIL work.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis appears problematic in places. Theorem 1 is stated as a sample complexity result for estimating the mean, but for bounded finite-population sampling the dependence on log |Omega| via a union bound over possible values is not justified for the stated goal. More seriously, in Theorem 2 the martingale expectation Z0 is set equal to the true population mean even though the estimator fixes two extreme samples and samples the rest from Omega excluding them; this estimator is generally biased unless additional assumptions hold. These issues weaken the claimed theoretical foundation.

The claim that adding one random 'median' sequence is theoretically guaranteed to lie near the center of the distribution is not convincing, especially with only one random sample. This is important because EDGE still estimates a distribution from only three samples.

The strongest quantitative validation uses only six selected classes and 90 enumerable sequences. This is useful as a controlled study, but it is a very small setting relative to realistic CIL benchmarks, and the selected 'first six classes' may not be representative.

In the classic large-scale CIL setting, ground-truth distributions are unavailable, so the evidence mainly shows that EDGE finds lower minima and higher maxima than RS, not necessarily that these are closer to true distributional boundaries or that the estimated mean/variance are calibrated.

The method relies on CLIP text similarity as a proxy for visual/task difficulty. The appendix discusses this thoughtfully, including medical domains, but the main protocol may be less reliable for datasets with ambiguous labels, non-visual class semantics, or domains poorly aligned with CLIP.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially phrases suggesting approximation of the full performance distribution or robust Gaussian estimation from three constructed sequences. The paper would be stronger if it framed EDGE primarily as boundary-aware stress testing plus compatibility reporting with RS.
